newsitem.title: FRANCE: France hopes troops will move into Zaire by weekend.
newsitem.headline: France hopes troops will move into Zaire by weekend.

text.p: France said on Thursday it hoped the first troops of a multinational force to help refugees in Zaire would be in place by the weekend.
It said French soldiers would secure the airport around the eastern town of Bukavu.

Paris also urged all U.N. member states to provide either soldiers or cash for the mission and said it wanted American, European and African deputy commanders alongside a Canadian general leading the planned force of several thousand troops.
"I hope that by the weekend we'll see the first soldiers on the ground," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told Europe 1 radio.

Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said later that "France will contribute to ensuring the safety of the platform at Bukavu." Bukavu, near the Rwandan border, has one of the main airports in eastern Zaire as a key staging post for the mission.

The United States agreed in principle on Wednesday to take part. U.S. forces intend to secure the airfield in Goma, farther north, as well as a three-mile (4.8 km) corridor to the Rwandan border in a bid to encourage the refugees to go home.

France, which has led calls for an international mission to help 1.2 million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi uprooted by fighting between Zaire and Tutsi rebels, has said it is ready to send between 1,500 and 2,000 soldiers, including 600 paratroopers able to go within 24 hours of U.N. approval.

Military sources said two-thirds of the French troops earmarked to go to Zaire would come from France with the remaining third drawn from among the 8,000 French troops already permanently garrisoned in Africa.
The paratroopers on alert are expected to come from the Eighth Marine Infantry Parachute Regiment, based in southwestern France, and would fly from Toulouse, the sources said.
They intervened successfully in the Central African Republic earlier this year to prop up that country's government, which is allied to Paris, when its own army mutinied.

De Charette met U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy, both in Paris for a peace meeting on Bosnia on Thursday, and noted a "broad convergence of views" on Zaire, Doutriaux said.

He said France wanted any U.N. Security Council resolution authorising the force to stress the over-riding humanitarian goals of the mission to ensure food, water and medicines reach Hutu refugees fleeing the fighting in eastern Zaire.

France also wanted the resolution to mention that voluntary contributions to the force should either be military or "a contribution to a special fund" to finance the sending of troops from developing countries, such as in Africa, he said.
The force is to be under the overall command of a Canadian general. "We want the Canadian commander to have three deputies, one European, one American and one African," Doutriaux said.
He said the Security Council resolution also should urge the staging of a peace conference in Africa's Great Lakes region to address underlying political problems.

De Charette also stressed that the force's sole task should be to ensure aid gets to the refugees. He rejected suggestions that it should, for instance, help repatriate refugees or seek to control Tutsi rebels.

Rwanda accuses France of being partisan after it sent 2,500 troops to Rwanda in 1994 to help stop Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Rwanda's government says the French operation helped Hutus escape to Zaire.
De Charette, who has repeatedly denied a pro-Hutu bias, said "terrible crimes" had been committed in Rwanda in 1994 and that "those who committed them must be lawfully tried."
